what_it_does: When chip designers lay out the millions of wires that connect components on a chip, they use a two-step process: global routing (planning rough wire paths across large regions called tiles) followed by detailed routing (fitting exact wire shapes into physical space). The global routing step must predict how congested each tile's wiring will become, but existing tools estimate that congestion using a fixed, pre-calculated number that ignores the actual shape of the wires and how tightly they can be packed together. This inaccuracy causes the global router to choose paths that later turn out to be impossible to physically wire, forcing expensive re-runs. The Dynamic Local Usage (DLU) model replaces the fixed estimate with one that accounts for exact wire geometry and the gaps required between wire tips, giving a much more accurate picture of how many wires can actually fit. New routing algorithms then use this improved congestion signal to pick better paths, and the model can also handle incremental updates such as when a pin (a connection point) is moved slightly.
